post.title: RAG vs Fine-Tuning: When to Use Each (and When to Combine Them)
post.subtitle: A practical decision guide with Python code for both paths — choose the right approach before you spend weeks building the wrong one.
post.brief:
📌 TL;DR Summary

Use RAG when facts change frequently and answers must be source-grounded.
Use fine-tuning when you need stable behavior: tone, format, and domain-specific reasoning.
Use RAG + fine-t

## Scenario context To use either tool well, you need to understand what each one actually changes about an LLM. **RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)** is a runtime architecture, not a training technique. The model's weights are never touched. Instead, at inference time, a retrieval layer fetches relevant documents or passages and injects them into the prompt as context. The model reads this context and uses it to answer. If the con… This walkthrough focuses on **Core Concepts First: Why RAG and Fine-Tuning Solve Different Problems**. Before making a design choice, clarify: - To use either tool well, you need to understand what each one actually changes about an LLM. - RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is a runtime architecture, not a training technique. - The model's weights are never touched. **Concepts in play:** vector-databases-rag, consistency-replication, database-indexing, vector-embeddings-and-similarity ## Stage 1 — Decision Matrix: RAG, Fine-Tuning, or Hybrid - *Applies **vector-databases-rag** to the decision above.* **Observable outcome:** You can explain how “Decision Matrix: RAG, Fine-Tuning, or Hybrid” changes the architecture or implementation path. ## Stage 2 — The Two Teams That Built the Wrong Thing - Six months ago, Team A finished a RAG pipeline to answer questions about their internal documentation. - They celebrated the launch and closed the sprint. - Two months into production, the numbers told a different story: recall was stuck at 60%, the LLM was writing responses in a tone that made every answer sound like a Wikipedia summary, and it kept confusing internal prod… - Engineers blamed the vector store. *Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.* **Observable outcome:** Engineers blamed the vector store. ## Stage 3 — Six Signals That Tell You Which Tool to Reach For - Before writing a single line of code, apply this scoring table. - Rate each factor for your situation. - Whichever column accumulates more check marks is the starting recommendation. - Three clear decision tiers emerge from this table: RAG only: Your knowledge is external and changes frequently. *Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.* **Observable outcome:** Three clear decision tiers emerge from this table: RAG only: Your knowledge is external and changes frequently. ## Stage 4 — Deep Dive: How RAG and Fine-Tuning Work Under the Hood - Both approaches improve LLM output, but through completely different mechanisms. - Understanding the internal machinery of each — before choosing — prevents the most expensive architectural mistakes. - RAG Internals: From Chunking to Re-Ranking Most teams treat RAG as a solved problem after they wire up an embedding model and a vector store. - Then they wonder why recall is 60%. *Applies **vector-embeddings-and-similarity** to the decision above.* ```mermaid flowchart TD Pretrained["Pretrained
Model

(Trainable)"] Finetune["Fine-tune on
Custom Data"] Result["Fine-tuned
Model"] Pretrained --> LoRA LoRA --> Finetune Finetune --> Result ``` **Observable outcome:** Then they wonder why recall is 60%. ## Stage 5 — Architecture and Workflow: How This Works in Production - The architecture decision affects far more than model quality. - It changes your deployment pipeline, observability strategy, incident response, and cost profile. - The diagram separates the two retrieval channels intentionally: dense search catches semantically similar passages even when query wording differs from document wording, while sparse BM25 catches exact product names, ve… - RRF fusion gives higher combined scores to documents that rank well in both channels, boosting precision without requiring a trained re-ranker at the fusion step. *Applies **vector-databases-rag** to the decision above.* ```mermaid graph TD A[User Query] --> B[Embed Query with Embedding Model] B --> C[Dense Vector Search in HNSW Index] A --> D[BM25 Sparse Keyword Search] C --> E[Merge Candidates via RRF Score Fusion] D --> E E --> F[CrossEncoder Re-Ranker] F --> G[Top-K Context Chunks Selected] G --> H[Prompt Assembly with System Instructions] H --> I[LLM Inference] I --> J[Grounded Response with Citations] ``` **Observable outcome:** RRF fusion gives higher combined scores to documents that rank well in both channels, boosting precision without requiring a trained re-ranker at the fusion step. ## Stage 6 — The LoRA Training and Serving Flow, Visualized - Training with LoRA involves freezing the base model and routing gradients only through the small adapter matrices. - Serving can either merge the adapter weights back into the base model for zero-latency overhead, or keep them separate and apply them dynamically when multiple adapters need to share a single base model. - The key insight from this flow is what does NOT appear in the gradient path: the frozen base model layers. - Because the base model parameters never receive gradient updates, there is no risk of catastrophic forgetting in those layers — the forgetting risk comes entirely from the LoRA adapter influencing the activation pattern… *Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.* ```mermaid graph TD A[Instruction-Formatted Training Examples] --> B[Tokenize with Chat Template] B --> C[Load Base Model in 4-bit via QLoRA] C --> D[Attach LoRA Adapter Layers to q-proj and v-proj] D --> E[Forward Pass - Frozen Base plus Trainable Adapter] E --> F[Compute Causal LM Loss] F --> G[Backprop Through Adapter Only] G --> H[Checkpoint Adapter Weights] H --> I[Merge Adapter into Base Model] I --> J[Serve with vLLM or HuggingFace TGI] ``` **Observable outcome:** Because the base model parameters never receive gradient updates, there is no risk of catastrophic forgetting in those layers — the forgetting risk comes entirely from the LoRA adapter influencing the activation pattern… ## End-to-end outcome After working through the stages, you should be able to explain: - - Use RAG when facts change frequently and answers must be source-grounded. - - Use fine-tuning when you need stable behavior: tone, format, and domain-specific reasoning. ## Alternatives considered ### Comparison: Cost, Latency, Maintenance, Freshness, and Control Quick takeaway: If your core risk is stale answers, start with RAG. ### Choose RAG when: - Your source of truth changes frequently. ### Choose Fine-Tuning when: - You need stable tone, output structure, and domain-specific response behavior. ### Choose Hybrid when: - You need both factual freshness and consistent communication style. ## Failure and degraded modes ### Seven Failure Modes: Symptoms, Root Causes, and Fixes -
